4. Comments:
Statistical analysis: The handling of multiple testing in large omics datasets is not clearly described. Without appropriate correction, the risk of false positives is high.Some baseline imbalances (e.g., higher IL-6 and triglycerides in the intervention group) complicate interpretation of intervention effects. Many results are reported primarily through p-values. Greater emphasis on effect sizes and clinical relevance would improve interpretation.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for these critical and constructive comments regarding the statistical analysis.
For the statistical methods in the omics analysis section, we first used the Wilcoxon rank sum test to analyze the differences between H-MPs and L-MPs in the baseline population. For the RCT population, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to analyze the differences among the four groups (the pre-intervention and post-intervention groups of the placebo group and the intervention group), and then the Tukey-Kramer post hoc test was conducted. The above content has been revised simultaneously in the section "Qualification and statistical analysis" of the manuscript: "In phenotypic and omics analyses, significant differences between the two groups were analyzed using independent sample T-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Significant differences among multiple groups were analyzed using one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Tukey-Kramer post hoc tests." (Page: 9, Line: 347)
Secondly, in the metagenomic analysis, the Wilcoxon rank sum test revealed that there were 23 significantly different bacterial genera between the H-MPs group and the L-MPs group (P < 0.05). However, after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (using the Benjamini-Hochberg method), the P-FDR of these 23 significantly different genera were not significant. Therefore, in the analysis of metagenomic data, in order to identify the significantly different bacteria between different groups while reducing the risk of false positives, we added the results of LEfSe differential discrimination analysis (Figure S4E and S4F). For plasma metabolomics, based on your suggestion, we used the FDR-corrected P-value instead of the original P-value to screen the differential metabolites between different groups. The detailed criteria are as follows: P-FDR < 0.25 and VIP > 1. The above content has been revised simultaneously in the "Qualification and statistical analysis" section of the manuscript: "In phenotypic and omics analyses, significant differences between the two groups were analyzed using independent sample T-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Significant differences among multiple groups were analyzed using one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Tukey-Kramer post hoc tests." (Page: 9, Line: 347); "The alpha diversity was evaluated by the calculated Shannon and Simpson indices. The beta diversity was assessed using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) based on the Bray-Curtis distances. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) was used to identify the differentially abundant taxa. For plasma metabolomics, the ropls package (Version 1.6.2) in R was used to perform principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) on the preprocessed data matrix. Significant differential metabolites were screened based on variable importance in projection (VIP) values and Student’s t-test from the OPLS-DA model. Differential metabolites were screened using the criteria: P-FDR < 0.25, and VIP > 1. Differential metabolites were annotated using the KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp/kegg/pathway.html) for metabolic pathway enrichment analysis. The gut microorganisms with P < 0.05, as well as the plasma metabolites with P-FDR < 0.25 and VIP > 1, were used for subsequent correlation analysis. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using the Python package scipy.stats, and Fisher’s exact test was used to identify the most relevant biological pathways associated with the experimental treatment. Spearman’s correlation coefficients were calculated to assess correlations between metabolites, species, and phenotypes, with coefficients > 0.2 and P < 0.05 considered significant. For omics research, the P-values were all corrected using FDR method (Benjamini & Hochberg). All other statistical analyses with P < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Effect sizes (Cohen’s d method) were presented along with statistical significance." (Page: 9, Line: 360);
"For the FSBPs and RCT populations, the taxonomic composition of the gut microbiota is presented in Figure S4A and S4B. At the genus level, attention was paid to the significantly differentially expressed genera with the highest relative abundance. Figure S4C shows that the relative abundance of Ruminococcus and Escherichia in the H-MPs was significantly lower than that in the L-MPs; However, there was no significant difference after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The LEfSe analysis also revealed that the Ruminococcus and Escherichia were the two bacterial genera that had the greatest impact on the differential effects between the H-MPs and L-MPs groups (Figure S4E). Furthermore, Figure S4D indicates that the relative abundances of bacterial genera such as Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium, and Phocaeicola significantly differed among the four groups. Further multiple comparisons revealed that the After-Int group had a significantly higher relative abundance of Faecalibacterium and Phocaeicola compared to the Base-Int group, whereas no significant difference in Bacteroides abundance was observed between these two groups (Figure S4G-I). The LEfSe analysis revealed that the Foetidibacter had the greatest impact on the differential effects between the four groups (Figure S4F)." (Page: 15, Line: 458)
The most important part is the multi-omics combined analysis section. We used a stepwise dimension reduction method to screen out potential key bacteria and metabolites. In the metagenomic analysis, the Wilcoxon rank sum test revealed that there were 507 significant differences in bacterial genera between the H-MPs group and the L-MPs group (P < 0.05). However, after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (using the Benjamini-Hochberg method), the P-FDR of these 507 significant differences in genera was all > 0.7. The possible reason might be that when annotating the metagenomic data to the "species" level, the types of intestinal microorganisms can reach over ten thousand. And the P values of the significant differences in bacteria between the H-MPs group and the L-MPs group were not particularly low, which might lead to the P values of the significant differences becoming very large after correction.
Our previous research also found this phenomenon[1]. Furthermore, for the significantly different bacterial species mentioned above, we will perform subsequent dimensionality reduction through the following steps: (1) conducting Spearman correlation analyses among the significantly altered bacterial species, metabolites, and host phenotypes, using a correlation coefficient (r) >0.2 and P < 0.05 as the screening criterion; and (2) integrating common correlation networks identified in both the baseline population and the RCT population. Therefore, in the first step of the metagenomic data analysis, as mentioned above, the P values of the significant differences in bacteria between the H-MPs group and the L-MPs group after FDR correction were all greater than 0.7. This led to our inability to perform the subsequent dimension reduction steps. Moreover, considering that in this step our aim was to screen out the bacteria with more significant relative differences under high exposure to MPs from the over ten thousand bacterial species annotated in the baseline population, for subsequent analysis steps. Therefore, in the multi-omics combined analysis process, we did not perform FDR correction for the metagenomic data. For the serum metabolome, the updated screening criteria were also P-FDR < 0.25 and VIP > 1, and a total of 144 significant difference metabolites were screened out.
Based on your comments and the above content, the "Results" sections of this manuscript have been re-written as follows: "Furthermore, significant alterations were observed in the abundance of 507 gut microbial species between the H-MPs and L-MPs groups; However, there was no significant difference after false discovery rate (FDR) correction." (Page: 15, Line: 473)
Regarding the phenomenon of baseline imbalances, we acknowledge that the baseline imbalances in certain parameters (e.g., IL-6 and triglycerides) pose a challenge for interpreting the intervention effects. As this was an observational baseline characteristic in our recruited cohort, we could not intervene to alter this distribution post-randomization. To reduce the impact of this cause in the analysis, we calculated the difference between the post-intervention and pre-intervention to analyze these outcome measures: "The pre-post differences within each group were calculated, and significant differences in change values between the two groups were analyzed using independent samples t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests." (Page: 9, Line: 350)
Regarding the results report section. We believe that your suggestion that the results should not be reported solely based on the P-value is very reasonable. The results should not only focus on whether there is a significant impact, but also on how significant this impact is. Effect sizes can compensate for the result misjudgments caused by over-reliance on the P-value. Therefore, we have revised the results section of the manuscript to ensure that effect sizes will be presented prominently along with statistical significance: "All other statistical analyses with P < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Effect sizes (Cohen’s d method) were presented along with statistical significance." (Page: 9, Line: 376) At the same time, we agree with your point that the importance of effect size and clinical relevance cannot be overstated. Therefore, based on your opinion and the modifications made to the above results, we have revised and expanded the discussion in this section, providing a more in-depth interpretation of the key correlations discovered, and not just focusing on the P-value: "Interestingly, following the intervention, the elevated levels of IL-6 in the After-Int group were alleviated, with a notably substantial effect size (P < 0.05, effect size = -0.576). Compared with the placebo group, the levels of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8) in the intervention group were significantly reduced following the intervention (P < 0.05), with effect sizes of -0.463, -0.576, and -0.529, respectively." (Page: 12, Line: 438)
Thank you again for these valuable suggestions, which have substantially improved the rigor and clarity of our manuscript.
Reference:
1. Liu S, Liu X, Guo J, et al. The Association Between Microplastics and Microbiota in Placentas and Meconium: The First Evidence in Humans. Environ Sci Technol. 2023 Nov 21;57(46):17774-17785.
5. Comments:
Interpretation: Some discussion points overstate causality (e.g., MPs "leading to" neurodegenerative pathways). These should be presented as associations or hypotheses. Proposed mechanistic chains (e.g., Sutterella abundance → lipid metabolism changes → systemic inflammation) remain speculative and should be presented as such. Statements about CP as a "protective strategy" are premature given the short timeframe, modest effect sizes, and absence of clinical endpoints.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable feedback concerning the interpretation of our results. We fully agree that the expression of the observed relationships in our study should be more precise and better reflect the correlational and exploratory nature of our research. In response to this comment, we have carefully revised the discussion section to ensure greater clarity and caution in interpreting findings, explicitly avoiding any language that might imply a direct causal relationship.
Firstly, during the revision process, we adopted a more stringent statistical approach for the microbiome analysis to address your concern in Comments 4. Under this optimized analytical framework, the significance of Sutterella diminished, while Staphylococcus was identified as the primary target genus. To ensure our conclusions are built on the most robust evidence, we have shifted our focus to Staphylococcus in the revised manuscript.
Secondly, regarding your points of "MPs leading to neurodegenerative pathways" and "Staphylococcus abundance → lipid metabolism changes → systemic inflammation", we have rephrased the "Abstract" and "Discussion" sections to reduce the emphasis on the causal relationships described therein: "The gut microorganism Staphylococcus and the plasma metabolite PC (22:5/0:0) were identified as relatively important potential targets in this protective effect." (Page: 1, Line: 27); "Notably, it could be speculated that intestinal Staphylococcus genus and plasma metabolite PC (22:5/0:0) were the important targets for CP interventions to mitigate the toxic effects associated with the high MP exposure, which deserve further research validation." (Page: 27, Line: 878); "These results suggest that exposure to higher MPs may be associated with alterations in gut microbiota function and the development of various cognitive-related diseases." (Page: 24, Line: 720); "Therefore, this study speculates that MP exposure may disrupt lipid and amino acid metabolism by altering the composition of gut microbiota, leading to the down-regulation of metabolites associated with the above pathways (primarily PC (22:5/0:0)). This disruption may be related to an imbalance in lipid metabolism and the promotion of systemic inflammation." (Page: 26, Line: 822)
Thirdly, we have toned down the conclusive language regarding the protective strategy of the intervention. The relevant statements in the "Discussion" section of this manuscript have been revised to clarify that, while our results show promising associative changes, the short-term duration, modest effect sizes, and lack of direct clinical endpoints mean that these findings are preliminary: "Given the early stage of this research and its limitations in duration, scale, and the scope of clinical indicators, further investigation is essential. Future work should prioritize conducting large-scale, long-term, and fully randomized human trials to verify the clinical effectiveness of CP protection strategies. Simultaneously, rigorous in vivo and in vitro experiments should be performed, along with targeted lipidomics research, to precisely quantify the dynamic changes of PC (22:5/0:0) and other glycerophospholipid metabolites at different time points, thus comprehensively exploring its protective rationale and potential mechanisms. Moreover, to accurately investigate the causal relationship between CP intervention and the alleviation of immune disorders associated with MP exposure, long-term CP intervention should be implemented in populations with higher levels of MP exposure. After a specific intervention period, the intervention should be ceased, and the changes in effects before and after the cessation should be analyzed to determine the causal relationship between the intervention and the outcome." (Page: 28, Line: 896) It is also described in the section on "Limitations": "Firstly, in the cross-sectional baseline study, measuring exposures and outcomes simultaneously prevents establishing temporality, thus precluding causal inference. The results obtained from strictly controlled RCT studies may have limited external validity. The potential intervention targets identified through correlation analysis are also speculative and still require further validation via in vivo or in vitro experiments."(Page: 28, Line: 911)
Furthermore, we also made careful revisions to other parts of the manuscript to avoid using causal language throughout the entire discussion. Specifically, we have replaced phrases such as "leading to" with more accurate terms like "associated with," "may contribute to," or "could suggest a potential link". For the unproven mechanism pathways proposed in the manuscript, the descriptive sections all indicated their speculative nature and were presented as a model for generating hypotheses for future research.
These changes have been implemented in the relevant sections of the manuscript to ensure our interpretations are appropriately cautious and aligned with the evidence presented.

Reviewer #2: This manuscript addresses an important and timely question: the population-level health impacts of microplastics (MP) exposure and a potential dietary mitigation strategy using a composite polyphenol (CP) formulation. Response:
Thank you for your comments. We really appreciate your efforts in reviewing our manuscript. We have revised the manuscript accordingly. Our point-by-point responses are detailed below.
1. Comments:

2. Comments:
Explain why 15 g/day was chosen (e.g., manufacturer recommendation, prior human clinical data, preclinical efficacy/tolerability data, or pilot tolerability studies) and provide supporting references or pilot data. If the dose is based on the manufacturer’s recommended serving, state this explicitly.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this important question regarding our dosage selection. The chosen dose was determined through a combination of factors, as detailed below:
The 15 g/day dose mentioned in the previous manuscript refers to the total amount of the intervention product administered to participants, which was taken three times a day, with each dose being one sachet of 5 g. The scientific rationale for this dose was based on its content of active compounds (mixed polyphenols). We conducted UPLC/MS analysis on the intervention product and determined that each sachet of 5 g contained 165 mg of polyphenols. That is, the 15 g of daily dosage can provide 465 mg of mixed polyphenols.
Our selection of the 465 mg/day target dose for mixed polyphenols was a deliberate decision based on several factors. First, we referred to the daily minimum intake recommended by the manufacturer, which is 2 sachets, containing 310 mg of polyphenols. This figure has been generally regarded as safe. However, to ensure a dose robust enough to produce an observable and clinically meaningful effect within our 28-day intervention period, we also reviewed the existing clinical literature. This review confirmed that polyphenol doses exceeding 1000 mg/day have been safely administered in human trials while demonstrating significant physiological effects[1,2]. Therefore, in consultation with the manufacturer, we selected a target dose of 465 mg/day. This dose was determined to be optimal, as it is higher than the minimum recommended (310 mg/day), which has the potential to enhance the beneficial effects, while remaining well within the established safety margins identified in the literature.
In summary, the intervention dose was not arbitrary. It was a scientifically justified decision derived from our target active dose of 465 mg/day of mixed polyphenols, which itself was informed by manufacturer guidelines, scientific literature, and expert consultation to balance the pursuit of efficacy with a paramount commitment to participant safety.

3. Comments:
Selection and detection of targeted microplastics (MPs):
a. Explain the criteria used to select the MPs in Table S2 (representativeness, prevalence in environment/human samples, polymer classes, particle size, expected exposure routes).
b. Clarify which of the targeted MPs were actually detected in participants’ samples and at what concentrations. Table S6 shows five of eleven, please disclose whether the other six were below detection limits or not analyzed.
c. If some targeted MPs were not detected, discuss implications for exposure–effect analyses and whether analyses should focus on the detected subset.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments regarding the selection and detection of targeted MPs. We have addressed your points as follows:
a. Explanation of the criteria used to select the target MPs:
Our selection of the 11 target polymers (PVC, PET, PE, PS, PP, PC, PA6, PA66, PLA, PMMA, and PBAT) was based on a comprehensive assessment of the following criteria:
Representativeness: The selected list is highly representative of global plastic production and consumption. It covers the five major commodity plastics (PE, PP, PVC, PS, and PET), which constitute the bulk of plastic waste. It also includes key engineering plastics (PC, PA6, PA66, and PMMA) valued for their performance in durable goods, and incorporates emerging bio-based and biodegradable plastics (PLA and PBAT) to reflect current market trends and their environmental relevance.
Prevalence in Environmental and Human Samples: These polymers, particularly PE, PP, PET, and PS, are among the most frequently identified MPs in diverse environmental matrices (e.g., water, sediment, air)[1, 2]and have been widely detected in human samples, including feces, blood, and lung tissue[3-5]. Targeting these prevalent MPs ensures our findings are comparable with the broader scientific literature and relevant to common human exposures.
Expected exposure pathways: The selected MPs are directly related to the main human exposure pathways. Oral intake may be the main pathway for MPs[6, 7]. The research has found that MPs have been widely detected in many of the foods we consume daily, such as drinking water, tea, salt, beer, beverages, seafood, sugar, and fruits. The main types of MPs are PET, PS, PA, and PE[8-11]. Furthermore, the processing, packaging, and handling stages of modern diets also extensively use plastics, which may also release additional MPs[11]. Beverage bottles, takeout boxes, plastic baby bottles, milk storage bags, and other food packaging containers all release MPs during use, mainly including PS, PE, PET, and PP[12-14]. It is equally important to note that the fibers and other material fragments (such as PET, PA6, PA66) present in textiles can also easily adhere to surfaces like food, thereby leading to ingestion through the mouth[15, 16]. Apart from oral exposure, inhalation is also one of the important ways for the population to come into contact with MPs. Current research has found that the MPs detected in indoor air and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of non-smokers mainly include PE, PET, and PP[17, 18]. Regarding the skin contact aspect for MPs, the research indicates that humans may be exposed to types of MPs such as PE and PS through the use of skin-cleaning products, medical applications, and other means[19, 20]. Nevertheless, many countries and organizations have issued regulations prohibiting the addition of MPs in cosmetics[21]. The risk of absorbing MPs or nanoplastics (NPs) through the skin exposure route is still unclear. It should be noted that the aforementioned types of MPs were also mainly detected in the population sample of this study.
Furthermore, it should be clarified that the 11 types of MPs we have selected for detection are also the upper limit that the current Py-GC/MS method can reach for detection (ASTM D8401-24). One limitation of the Py-GC/MS method is that it cannot provide information on the particle size of MPs. Since this is a destructive study, we also look forward to the development of more comprehensive Py-GC/MS detection methods for various polymer types, as well as combined detection methods.
b. Clarification of which targeted MPs were detected in participant samples:
We analyzed all 11 targeted MP types as planned. However, the detection frequencies varied significantly among the polymers. Five of the MPs were consistently detected in participant samples, each with a detection frequency greater than 70%. These were: polyethylene (PE), polyamide 66 (PA66), polystyrene (PS), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) 56.34 μg/g dw, with an median value of 23.51 (11.48, 42.66) μg/g dw, 63.95 (37.01, 94.03) μg/g dw, 0.85 (0.42, 1.61) μg/g dw, 9.64 (3.83, 27.34) μg/g dw and 56.34 (39.72, 72.13) μg/g dw, respectively. The above results are also described in Table S2 and Table S3 of this manuscript. The remaining six targeted MPs were either not detected or were detected at very low frequencies. To enhance transparency, we have updated Table S2 in the supplementary materials to include the specific detection frequencies for all 11 targeted MPs.
c. Discussion of implications for undetected MPs in exposure-effect analyses:
We agree that the handling of non-detected compounds is a critical aspect of the analysis. Given that the six MPs with very low detection rates constitute highly censored data, including them in the exposure-effect models would introduce substantial statistical bias and could lead to unreliable conclusions. For the undetected data, we usually have two approaches. One is to use multiple interpolations. However, when the proportion of missing data exceeds 70%, the reliability and accuracy of the data will be severely compromised[1, 2]. Secondly, the undetected data can be replaced by the detection limit or the minimum value. However, too much duplicate data in the statistical model may cause deviations in the analysis results[3]. Therefore, to ensure the statistical robustness and validity of our findings, we focused the subsequent statistical analyses exclusively on the five MPs with reliable detection rates of 70%.
The important point is that the absence of detection of other types of MPs in our sample might indicate that exposure to these polymers was negligible within this cohort, or that their concentrations were below the limit of detection of our analytical method. Therefore, this suggests that they may have limited relevance to the health outcomes examined in this specific study population.
We want to emphasize that all 11 MPs were included in the initial analytical screening, and none were arbitrarily omitted. We have revised the "Methods" and "Results" sections to provide a clearer description of our analytical process and the criteria used for including MPs in the final statistical analyses: "Fecal samples from all 151 participants were tested for the presence of these 11 types of polymers." (Page: 7, Line: 264); "Other types of MPs (PP, PMMA, PC, PA6, PLA and PBAT) were not detected or had a detection rate of less than 70%." (Page: 10, Line: 387)
Thank you once again for your constructive review, which has significantly strengthened the quality and clarity of our manuscript.

4. Comments:
Exposure route and source attribution. The manuscript mentions PVC is widely used in construction materials. Provide discussion and (if available) rationale or evidence on likely exposure pathways for the MPs measured (oral/dietary ingestion, inhalation, dermal). State whether the measured MPs in the biological matrix are most plausibly reflecting dietary intake, inhalation, dust ingestion, or mixed routes. Discuss how non-dietary exposure routes could influence gut microbiome-mediated effects (for example, inhaled MPs that are swallowed via mucociliary clearance).
Response:
Thank you for your guidance. We believe that your opinion is extremely important for the structure improvement of the risk assessment section of this manuscript. The responses and revisions we have made are as follows:
Firstly, concerning the possible exposure pathways of the detected MPs that you raised, we have addressed this in Comment 3. The MPs we selected are directly relevant to the major human exposure pathways. We analyzed all 11 targeted types of MPs as planned. In the fecal samples of the participants, five types—PE, PA66, PS, PET, and PVC—were predominantly detected, with detection frequencies exceeding 70% for each. The exact origins of these MPs remain difficult to trace; potential sources could be cautiously hypothesized. Among them, PS, PET, and PE are commonly used in food packaging and disposable products, suggesting that dietary intake is likely the primary exposure route. These polymers have been frequently detected in various food items and during the use of plastic food containers[1-7]. Furthermore, PA66 is widely used in textiles, industrial components, and electronic devices. Research indicates that fibers and fragments from synthetic textiles (e.g., PA6, PA66) could become airborne or adhere to food surfaces, leading to ingestion via ingestion and inhalation pathways[8-9]. Additionally, PVC is extensively employed in construction materials, while PET is also utilized in engineering plastics and household goods. Studies report that PET and PVC are among the most prevalent polymer types in indoor air, increasing the risk of inhalation exposure[10]. PE and PS are often included in personal care products and medical formulations, raising concerns about dermal exposure[11-12]. Nevertheless, many countries and organizations have issued regulations prohibiting the addition of MPs to cosmetics[13]. The risk of absorbing MPs or nanoplastics (NPs) through the skin exposure route is still unclear and warrants further investigation.
Secondly, concerning the most likely sources of MPs measured in biological samples—whether they derive from dietary intake, inhalation, dust intake, or a combination of these pathways—we hypothesize that the mixed pathway is the primary route of exposure. The reasons are as follows: First, MPs have been detected in various foods consumed daily by humans, which suggests humans are continuously ingesting large amounts of MPs orally[1-4]. Research further suggests that the majority of MPs detected in feces originate from the fraction that is ingested but not absorbed[18]. Moreover, the levels of MPs detected in feces also show a significant correlation with human diet and the degree of food processing[14]. Second, humans breathe constantly, and it has been widely proven that the air is filled with MPs[15]. For MPs inhaled through the respiratory system, some may enter the cardiovascular system and be transported via the bloodstream[16]. Subsequently, some MPs in the blood can be filtered by the spleen and cleared into the intestinal tract. Furthermore, studies have shown that MPs deposited in the lungs may be transferred to the esophagus through the mucosal cilia clearance mechanism[17]. Crucially, the types of MPs detected in large quantities in our fecal samples correspond to the types reported to be potentially inhaled. Finally, although some studies suggest that skin exposure is a potential route for MPs, due to the protective function of the skin, it is not as widespread as ingestion and inhalation. Only a small portion of nanoplastics, synthetic fibers, or monomers can penetrate (with the exception of damaged skin)[18].
Therefore, based on these findings, we reasonably speculate that the MPs detected in the feces of the population in this study likely originate from multiple pathways. However, since this is not the main research direction and result of this study, this content remains speculative. We plan to conduct further research in this direction in the future. The above was also described in detail in the "Discussion" section of our manuscript:
"In addition, PVC and PA66 exhibited the highest detection rates and concentrations in our study, followed by PE, PS, and PET. Consistently, Song et al. and Ke et al. also found that the top three polymers with the highest detection rates of MPs in human fecal samples included PVC and PE[25]. Detection of MPs in feces could be associated with the specific types of plastics to which individuals are routinely exposed. PE, PS, and PET is commonly employed in food containers, disposable products, etc. Many of the foods and beverages consumed daily—such as drinking water, tea, salt, beer, soft drinks, seafood, sugar, and fruits—are found to contain MPs, primarily in the types of PET, PS, PA, and PE[32, 33].
In addition, modern food processing, packaging, and handling practices may release MPs, including PS, PE, PET, and PP[34, 35]. Furthermore, PA66 is widely used in textiles, industrial components, and electronic devices. Research indicates that fibers and fragments from synthetic textiles (e.g., PA6, PA66) could become suspended in the air or adhere to food surfaces, leading to ingestion via ingestion and inhalation pathways[36, 37]. PVC is extensively employed in construction materials, while PET is also utilized in engineering plastics and household goods. Studies report that PET and PVC are among the most prevalent polymer types detected in indoor air, increasing the risk of inhalation exposure[38]. PE and PS are often included in personal care products and medical formulations, raising concerns about dermal exposure[39, 40]. Collectively, these findings suggest that the MPs detected in the fecal samples of this study likely originate from multiple exposure pathways. However, this conclusion remains preliminary and warrants further investigation to enable a more comprehensive understanding." (Page: 22, Line: 645)
Finally, regarding the discussion on how non-dietary exposure methods affect the effects mediated by the intestinal microbiome, after our literature review and discussion, we agree that this perspective is highly important for enhancing the depth of the manuscript. As you mentioned, and as stated above, MPs accumulated in the human digestive tract may partially originate from respiratory intake. During the migration of MPs, their shape and the loads of other microorganisms/pollutants will change[18, 20], which could impact the intestinal microbiome. However, such studies are currently lacking, and the above results remain speculative. Consequently, further in-depth research is still required. Therefore, we have added a description of the possible effects of non-dietary exposure methods on the intestinal microbiome to the "Discussion" section of this manuscript:
"Regarding the aforementioned MPs that come into contact with the gut microbial in the intestines, non-dietary exposure routes are as critical as oral intake. MPs detected in human feces may partly originate from inhalation via the respiratory tract, subsequently entering the gastrointestinal tract through systemic circulation or mucociliary clearance mechanisms[51]. During their translocation, the physical characteristics of MPs and their associated loads of microorganisms or pollutants may change, potentially exerting additional impacts on the composition and function of the gut microbiota[51, 52]." (Page: 24, Line: 724)

5. Comments:
The authors report gut microbiome changes (notably Sutterella) associated with MP exposure and CP effects. Explicitly discuss whether microbiome alterations are more likely a cause or a consequence of MP exposure (or of host response to MPs). Clarify limitations of cross-sectional associations and the RCT for causal inference, and propose approaches to test directionality.
Response:
Thank you for your guidance. Regarding the questions you raised, our response and the revisions made to the manuscript are as follows:
Firstly, during the revision process, we adopted a more stringent statistical approach for the microbiome analysis to address concerns raised by another reviewer. Under this optimized analytical framework, the significance of Sutterella diminished, while Staphylococcus was identified as the primary target genus. To ensure our conclusions are built on the most robust evidence, we have shifted our focus to Staphylococcus in the revised manuscript. Regarding the question of whether the changes in the microbial community are more likely to be the cause or the result of MP exposure, our discussion is as follows. On one hand, there is already extensive research evidence on the impact of MP exposure on the intestinal microbiome. Animal studies have shown that MP exposure can affect the structure and function of the intestinal microbiota, altering the abundance of beneficial and opportunistic pathogenic bacteria[1]. Furthermore, in vitro experiments have provided additional verification of the impact of MP exposure on the intestinal microbiome[2].
On the other hand, the intestinal microbiome has also been found to potentially affect the absorption and excretion of MPs. Studies have discovered that specific bacterial species in the intestine have the potential to degrade MPs, such as PET and ester-based polyurethanes (PUR), consequently influencing the size, type, and abundance of the accumulated MPs[3,4]. Crucially, research suggests that MPs may affect the communication between the host's intestines and the intestinal microbiota, thereby altering the expression of intestinal genes and the composition and structure of the intestinal microbiota[5]. Moreover, existing studies highlight that the intestinal microbiota can influence the host, and the host can also influence the intestinal microbiota[6-8]. Therefore, based on these results, we reasonably speculate that the relationship among MP exposure, changes in the intestinal microbiota, and the host's response is not a simple one-way transmission. Instead, there is a bidirectional communication mechanism at play.
In line with your comments and the above findings, we have revised and detailedly described this "Discussion" section of the manuscript: "The relationship between MP exposure, alterations in the gut microbiota, and host responses is likely not a unidirectional process, but rather involves a bidirectional interaction. Evidence from animal and in vitro studies has demonstrated that MP exposure could disrupt the composition and function of the gut microbiota[53, 54]. Conversely, the gut microbiota may influence the absorption, distribution, and excretion of MPs. Certain bacterial species in the gut have been shown to possess the capacity to degrade MPs[12, 55, 56]. Research reports indicate that MPs may interfere with host-microbiota crosstalk in the gut, leading to altered expression of intestinal genes and shifts in microbial community structure[57]. However, further investigation is required to confirm these findings and elucidate the underlying mechanisms." (Page: 24, Line: 732)
Secondly, we have, as per your instructions, incorporated relevant descriptions regarding the limitations of cross-sectional correlational studies and the role of randomized controlled trials in causal inference into the “Limitations” section of this manuscript: "Firstly, in the cross-sectional baseline study, measuring exposures and outcomes simultaneously prevents establishing temporality, thus precluding causal inference. The results obtained from strictly controlled RCT studies may have limited external validity. The potential intervention targets identified through correlation analysis are also speculative and still require further validation via in vivo or in vitro experiments. Additionally, for the RCT study, the intervention period was relatively short (28 days), the sample size was relatively limited (101 participants), and the participants were generally young, in good health, and predominantly female. This might account for the lack of significant changes observed in other clinical indicators, which limited the depth of our analysis and might also restrict the general applicability of the research results." (Page: 28, Line: 911)
Furthermore, in the "Discussion" section of the manuscript, we have added methods for testing the directionality of causal inferences in future research: "Given the early stage of this research and its limitations in duration, scale, and the scope of clinical indicators, further investigation is essential. Future work should prioritize conducting large-scale, long-term, and fully randomized human trials to verify the clinical effectiveness of CP protection strategies. Simultaneously, rigorous in vivo and in vitro experiments should be performed, along with targeted lipidomics research, to precisely quantify the dynamic changes of PC (22:5/0:0) and other glycerophospholipid metabolites at different time points, thus comprehensively exploring its protective rationale and potential mechanisms. Moreover, to accurately investigate the causal relationship between CP intervention and the alleviation of immune disorders associated with MP exposure, long-term CP intervention should be implemented in populations with higher levels of MP exposure. After a specific intervention period, the intervention should be ceased, and the changes in effects before and after the cessation should be analyzed to determine the causal relationship between the intervention and the outcome." (Page: 28, Line: 896)

6. Comments:
The manuscript states plasma cholesterol and LDL tended to increase with MP exposure, citing supporting studies. However, some preclinical reports (e.g., Lu L, Wan Z, Luo T, Fu Z, Jin Y. c. Clarify how the present human data fit within this heterogeneous literature.
Response:
Thank you for this excellent suggestion. We agree that a more nuanced discussion is needed. To address this, we have revised the manuscript to explicitly acknowledge the conflicting evidence, offer potential explanations for the discrepancies, and better position our human data within the existing literature.
a. Based on your suggestions, we have made revisions to the "Discussion" section of this manuscript, explicitly acknowledging the existence of contradictory evidence: "Several in vivo studies have also shown that exposure to both PS- and PE-MPs could lead to elevated serum CHO and LDL levels[42, 43]. It is noteworthy that the animal study conducted by Liu et al. reported divergent lipid-related outcomes compared to our findings, as both hepatic triglyceride (TG) and total cholesterol (TCH) levels were reduced[44]." (Page: 23, Line: 673)
b. The reasons you have proposed for the aforementioned contradictions might stem from species differences, polymer types, particle size, dosage, exposure route, diet, duration, which are very reasonable and important. Extrapolating the results of animal experiments to humans involves risks.
1. The doses, types, and particle sizes of the particles used in animal experiments are significantly different from the real situation. 2. We are exposed to mixed types of exposure (through the mouth, through breathing, etc.) every day, but the exposure methods used in animal experiments are usually oral. 3. The duration of animal experiments is generally only one month, but an adult may have been exposed to low doses continuously for a longer period of time. 4. Due to cost reasons, the sample size of most animal experiments is smaller than that of this study, and so on. Therefore, these differences may be the reason why our research results cannot be fully verified with animal studies. The above content is also described in the "Discussion" section of this manuscript: "These discrepancies may stem from multiple factors, such as variations in experimental models, exposure doses, and the types of exposure MPs. It is important to recognize the potential inconsistency between animal and human studies, which underscores the need for cautious interpretation of the results when extrapolating across species." (Page: 23, Line: 677)
c. It should be noted that currently, there are no similar studies conducted in a population setting. Therefore, our research results can only be compared with those of some animal studies or in vitro studies. As mentioned earlier, this may lead to the discovery of significantly different results. we believe that although there are differences between human data and previous animal study results, these pieces of evidence together indicate that MPs exposure will continuously lead to lipid metabolism disorders. The above content is also described in detail in the "Discussion" section of our manuscript: "Despite these varied outcomes, the collective evidence suggests that MP exposure may potentially contribute to lipid metabolism disorders. This disruption may manifest as a pro-atherogenic profile, underscoring the need for further research to elucidate the underlying mechanisms in humans." (Page: 23, Line: 681)
We are grateful for the opportunity to improve our manuscript and believe this change has significantly strengthened the discussion.
7. Comments:
Intervention duration and biological relevance of significant endpoints. A 28-day intervention is short for many cardiometabolic outcomes. The authors already note lack of changes in many clinical indicators. Please discuss whether the significant molecular/microbiome/metabolite changes (e.g., Sutterella and PC (22:5/0:0)) are likely to be transient biomarkers or plausibly predictive of longer-term clinical effects. State explicitly that these molecular changes require replication and longer-term follow-up for clinical interpretation.
Response:
Thank you for your question. We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comments on the trial duration. Reviewer 1 also raised this crucial issue in comment 3. The trial duration was determined based on practical constraints, including resource availability and feasibility for an initial investigation. We fully acknowledge that the 28-day intervention is a limitation for observing long-term health outcomes. To address this, we proactively increased the daily polyphenol dosage within the safe range to maximize the potential for a detectable effect within the study period. It should be noted that a larger or longer study would have incurred prohibitive costs, and we chose to invest our resources in deep, mechanistic analyses (such as multi-omics) rather than spreading them more thinly across a larger cohort. Furthermore, the 28-day timeframe was chosen to promote high participant compliance and minimize the risk of attrition, which often compromises longer-term studies. We fully agree that a 28-day intervention is generally insufficient to elicit stable clinical improvements in many cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes—such as blood lipids and blood glucose—which have been described in the "Discussion" and "Limitations" section of this manuscript:
"Additionally, no significant improvements were observed in plasma CHO and LDL indicators following CP intervention. This weakens the interpretability of these findings, which may potentially be attributed to the relatively brief duration of our intervention." (Page: 23, Line: 696);
"Given the early stage of this research and its limitations in duration, scale, and the scope of clinical indicators, further investigation is essential. Future work should prioritize conducting large-scale, long-term, and fully randomized human trials to verify the clinical effectiveness of CP protection strategies. Simultaneously, rigorous in vivo and in vitro experiments should be performed, along with targeted lipidomics research, to precisely quantify the dynamic changes of PC (22:5/0:0) and other glycerophospholipid metabolites at different time points, thus comprehensively exploring its protective rationale and potential mechanisms. Moreover, to accurately investigate the causal relationship between CP intervention and the alleviation of immune disorders associated with MP exposure, long-term CP intervention should be implemented in populations with higher levels of MP exposure. After a specific intervention period, the intervention should be ceased, and the changes in effects before and after the cessation should be analyzed to determine the causal relationship between the intervention and the outcome." (Page: 28, Line: 896); "Additionally, for the RCT study, the intervention period was relatively short (28 days), the sample size was relatively limited (101 participants), and the participants were generally young, in good health, and predominantly female. This might account for the lack of significant changes observed in other clinical indicators, which limited the depth of our analysis and might also restrict the general applicability of the research results." (Page: 28, Line: 915)
As is mentioned in response for comments 5, we have shifted our focus from Sutterella to Staphylococcus in the revised manuscript. Our research suggests that the intestinal microbe Staphylococcus and the plasma metabolite PC (22:5/0:0) may serve as potential targets for polyphenol intervention against MP-induced immune dysregulation. The observation that many clinical indicators remained unchanged, despite significant shifts in specific microbes and metabolites, warrants a discussion on whether these changes represent transient biomarkers or predictors of long-term clinical outcomes. In response to this viewpoint, we provided a detailed elaboration in the "Discussion" section, offering cautious interpretations of the observed molecular, microbial, and metabolite markers. We clarified that these markers may represent either transient responses to short-term exposure or early indicators of potential long-term biological pathways, while emphasizing that current evidence remains insufficient to support their use as direct predictors of long-term clinical outcomes:
"However, it should be noted that this study did not observe significant clinical improvements in most cardiovascular outcomes. Therefore, the interpretation of the aforementioned potential biomarkers should be approached with caution. The short-term changes observed may have two implications: on one hand, they may represent only a transient response to the intervention, reflecting reversible, short-term adjustments in gut ecology or metabolism; on the other hand, they may also serve as early biological signals that, if sustained over time, could contribute to longer-term physiological adaptations and ultimately influence clinical endpoints." (Page: 27, Line: 881)
Furthermore, we believe that the findings based on multi-omics are only preliminary. To clearly identify these molecular changes and their associated clinical indicators, further in vivo and in vitro/experimental studies, repeated research, and longer-term follow-ups are needed to verify. The above content is also elaborated in the "Discussion" section of the manuscript: "Given the early stage of this research and its limitations in duration, scale, and the scope of clinical indicators, further investigation is essential. Future work should prioritize conducting large-scale, long-term, and fully randomized human trials to verify the clinical effectiveness of CP protection strategies. Simultaneously, rigorous in vivo and in vitro experiments should be performed, along with targeted lipidomics research, to precisely quantify the dynamic changes of PC (22:5/0:0) and other glycerophospholipid metabolites at different time points, thus comprehensively exploring its protective rationale and potential mechanisms. Moreover, to accurately investigate the causal relationship between CP intervention and the alleviation of immune disorders associated with MP exposure, long-term CP intervention should be implemented in populations with higher levels of MP exposure. After a specific intervention period, the intervention should be ceased, and the changes in effects before and after the cessation should be analyzed to determine the causal relationship between the intervention and the outcome." (Page: 28, Line: 896)

Reviewer #3: The submitted work assessed the effects of dietary supplementation with composite polyphenols on microplastic exposure-related immune disturbances by a two-phase population trial. Overall, the 2 clinical studies were conducted rigorously, avoiding any major biases. The chosen methods are up-to -date, relevant, and well-described. The advanced statistical analyses require review by a qualified biostatistician, which I am not. The manuscript is clear, well-structured, and easy to understand, except for the difficulty in reading the figures which are very small and of poor quality (they are rarely readable even when enlarged).
Firstly, the authors performed a pilot population study with 75 participants in low MP exposure group and 76 participants in high MP exposure group. Microplastic were quantified in feces samples by Py-GC/MS. This study provides the first population-based evidence that MP exposure is associated with decreased blood levels of Il1b, Il-2, Il-10, Il-13, monocytes and increased levels of IFN-g, cholesterol and HDL. The weight of each MP polymer on the immune-inflammatory parameters was also analyzed. Differentially expressed fecal bacterial strains and pathways, and differential blood metabolites and pathways, associated with MP exposure in this pilot population study were identified. The mechanisms potentially involved are highlighted by integrated multi-omic analysis between plasma metabolome, fecal metagenome and host phenotype. These results are extremely important because they start to fill the knowledge gap on the effects of microplastic exposure in humans directly. This type of clinical data is highly anticipated by the scientific community and by society.
Second, the authors performed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled intervention trial to evaluate the protective effects of composite polyphenol supplementation on the adverse effects induced by microplastic exposure. As the adverse effects of MP exposure in healthy population are low, this part was really challenging but the in-depth analyses performed allowed the authors to identify Sutterella and plasma metabolite phosphatidylcholine (22:5/0:0) as key targets of mitigation of MP associated toxic effects by CP intervention.
Globally, the conclusions are supported by the results but I have few comments aiming to improve the manuscript.

Thank you for your question.
During the process of establishing the pre-treatment method, we used the ATR-FTIR method to conduct qualitative detection on the samples. Attenuated total reflection (ATR) is a testing method for FTIR, which has high sensitivity in detecting changes in the surface molecular groups of the samples. It is an effective means for identifying whether chemical reactions occur in MPs during the pre-treatment process. As shown in Figure 1, after the MPs PE, PP, PS, PMMA, PET, PC, PA, and PVC were immersed in 68% nitric acid at room temperature for 48 hours and then reacted at 110 °C for 3 hours, the FTIR spectra showed no significant changes. This indicates that the above reaction conditions do not affect the qualitative determination of microplastics PE, PP, PS, PMMA, PET, PC, and PVC. The pre-treatment process does not lead to the degradation of MPs. To further ensure that the degradation and loss of MPs are minimized during the pre-treatment process, we tested the recovery rate of the entire pre-treatment process to ensure the reliability of the pre-treatment method: "Table S2 lists the detection limits of the Py-GC/MS method and the pre-treatment recovery rates of low, medium and high concentrations of MPs spiking amounts." (Page: 28, Line: 920)
We fully agree with your emphasis on the significance of the size range of MPs detected in fecal samples. However, since we used the Py-GC/MS method for the detection, this method can obtain the mass of MPs, but as it is a destructive method, it will lose the information about the particle size of MPs and thus cannot obtain the size range of MPs in human feces. Based on your suggestion, we have discussed this point in the "Limitations" section of the discussion: "Due to the application of the Py-GC/MS method, it is also unable to obtain certain key information about MPs, such as particle size, color, and shape, which may be crucial in assessing their toxicity." Response:
Thank you very much for your valuable suggestions. We agree that in the original manuscript, we failed to adequately explain the reasons for choosing Ruminoccocus, Phocaeicola and Bacteroides as the main subjects of discussion. This indeed requires further elaboration.
We acknowledge that as stated in comment 11 that in both the H-MPs and L-MPs groups (involving Ruminoccocus), as well as among the four CP intervention groups (involving Phocaeicola and Bacteroides), a large number of differentially expressed bacterial genera were identified in the study.
Given the numerous different bacterial genera, it is difficult for us to directly determine which genera are biologically "more important". Therefore, we referred to the screening strategy adopted in other related metagenomic studies [1-4]: we selected the genera with the highest relative abundance among all those showing statistically significant differences for in-depth analysis.
The reason we adopted this standard is that these bacterial genera not only have a high abundance (possibly playing a fundamental role in the intestinal ecosystem), but also their abundance is significantly influenced by MPs exposure or CP intervention. Therefore, we can reasonably infer that these genera may be the most affected and crucial groups under our experimental conditions.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.
